title: Detraining: Loss of Training-Induced Physiological and Performance Adaptations. Part II: Long Term Insufficient Training Stimulus
population: Athletes and recently trained individuals; long-term (over 4 weeks) insufficient training
findings: VO2max of athletes declines markedly but remains above control values in long-term detraining, whereas recently acquired VO2max gains are completely lost.

Capillarisation, arterial-venous O2 difference and oxidative enzymes decline in athletes and are completely reversed in recently trained individuals; the lactate threshold is lowered but remains above untrained values in the highly trained.
Force production declines slowly, usually staying above control values for very long periods.

Losses can be avoided or limited by reduced-training strategies if intensity is maintained and frequency reduced only moderately; volume can be cut markedly. Athletes should use similar-mode exercise; moderately trained individuals may also benefit from dissimilar-mode cross-training.
limitations: Narrative review; no quantified loss rates in the abstract; not run-specific.
implications: Differentiate returning athletes by training history: after more than 4 weeks off, long-trained athletes keep part of their fitness (restart higher), whereas runners with only recent gains lose all of them (restart with run-walk and novice caps).
For planned reduced-training periods, keep intensity and cut volume heavily and frequency modestly; prefer same-mode work, with cross-training as a fallback when running is unsafe.

verification.notes: Own re-fetch: Crossref title (Part II), Sports Medicine 2000, 2 authors. Abstract matches. Added the similar-mode vs dissimilar-mode nuance.
